source_refs.note: Topic printed as 5.3, printed pages 161-163: the mechanism and disadvantages of photorespiration, C-4 photosynthesis and CAM metabolism.

blocks.text: The respiratory activity that occurs in green cells in the presence of light, resulting in the release of carbon dioxide, is photorespiration. It needs oxygen and produces CO2 and H2O like aerobic respiration, but no ATP is produced.

blocks.title: Recalling
blocks.text: During carbon fixation rubisco combines three molecules of CO2 with three molecules of RuBP and makes six molecules of 3-phosphoglyceric acid (3-PGA).

RuBP carboxylase (rubisco) catalyses the addition of CO2 to RuBP to make phosphoglyceric acid (phosphoglycerate), which is further reduced to form glucose. But when the relative concentration of CO2 decreases and there is more oxygen in the leaf cells, rubisco adds O2 to RuBP instead of CO2. RuBP then breaks into two molecules, one phosphoglycerate and one phosphoglycolate (a two-carbon molecule).

Phosphoglycolate is converted into glycolate, which moves from the chloroplast to a peroxisome. There it is metabolised to glyoxylate using O2, a reaction that also produces toxic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Glyoxylate is converted to glycine, which is transported to a mitochondrion, where two molecules of glycine form one molecule of serine. Serine is transported to the peroxisome and converted to glycerate; glycerate moves to the chloroplast, where it is changed to phosphoglycerate, which can re-enter the Calvin cycle.

blocks.alt: Three organelles. In the chloroplast O2 joins RuBP, which gives phosphoglycerate (to G3P and back to RuBP) and phosphoglycolate; phosphoglycolate takes in H2O and loses Pi to give glycolate. In the peroxisome glycolate, using O2 and releasing H2O2, gives glyoxylate, then glycine. In the mitochondrion glycine gives serine. Serine returns to the peroxisome and becomes glycerate, which goes back to the chloroplast as phosphoglycerate.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 5.21 marks H2O2 at the chloroplast step from phosphoglycolate to glycolate and ends the glycerate arrow at phosphoglycolate. At that step H2O is used and Pi is released, and glycerate is converted back to phosphoglycerate (as the book's text says), as drawn above.

Plants that use the Calvin cycle to fix carbon are C-3 plants. When photorespiration occurs in them, they lose between 25 and 50 percent of their fixed carbon, which reduces their yields. The rate of photorespiration also depends on temperature: at higher temperatures the oxidative activity of rubisco increases more than its carbon-fixing activity. In tropical climates, especially where the temperature is often above 28 degrees Celsius, the problem is severe and has a major negative impact on agricultural yields.

blocks.title: How the problem arose
blocks.text: When photosynthesis first evolved there was little oxygen in the atmosphere, so there was little or no photorespiration. After millions of years free O2 accumulated in the atmosphere and competition started between CO2 and O2 for the same active site of rubisco. That led to the problem photorespiration now poses.
Adaptations to the problem of photorespiration
Plants of warmer climates evolved two ways to deal with photorespiration: C-4 photosynthesis and CAM metabolism. C-4 and CAM plants carry out C-4 as well as C-3 photosynthesis.

Some plants, including the grasses corn, sugarcane and sorghum and about two dozen other plant groups, run a special pathway called C-4 photosynthesis in addition to the normal Calvin cycle. In their leaves the mesophyll cells have fewer air spaces, and the enzymes of the Calvin cycle are deposited mainly in specialised bundle-sheath cells, which are impermeable to CO2.

In C-4 photosynthesis, in the mesophyll cells, CO2 is attached to the three-carbon molecule phosphoenol pyruvic acid, forming the four-carbon oxaloacetic acid; because this first product has four carbons the process is called C-4 photosynthesis and the plants C-4 plants. Oxaloacetic acid is converted to malic acid using NADH, and malic acid is transported to an adjacent bundle-sheath cell, where it is broken down to pyruvic acid and CO2. These cells can hold CO2, so its concentration rises and they run the Calvin cycle instead of photorespiration. The pyruvic acid returns to the mesophyll cell and is converted again to phosphoenol pyruvic acid using an ATP.

blocks.alt: Left, C-3 Photosynthesis: in a mesophyll cell CO2 enters the Calvin cycle with RuBP and sugar leaves. Right, C-4 Photosynthesis: in the mesophyll cell CO2 joins phosphoenol pyruvic acid (3-C) to form oxaloacetic acid (4-C), which becomes malic acid (4-C); malic acid passes into the bundle sheath cell and splits into CO2, which enters the Calvin cycle with RuBP to make sugar, and pyruvic acid (3-C), which returns to the mesophyll cell and becomes phosphoenol pyruvic acid again.

blocks.title: The cost of C-4
blocks.text: In C-4 photosynthesis the energy cost of making a glucose molecule is almost double. But in hot climates, where photorespiration would otherwise remove more than half the carbon fixed, it is the best compromise available.

In hot climates many succulent plants such as cacti, pineapples and some other plant groups perform crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, named after the plant family Crassulaceae in which it was first discovered. In these plants the stomata open during the night and close during the day. Closing the stomata by day prevents the loss of water and the removal of CO2, so the rate of photorespiration is reduced by the high concentration of carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide needed to make sugar is provided from organic molecules made the night before. Like C-4 plants, these plants use both the C-4 and the C-3 pathways.
